subproblem.title: Cayley derivative formulas and their reciprocal product
subproblem.statement: Define φ(u)=i(1+u)/(1−u) and ψ(u)=(u−i)/(u+i) on ℂ using total complex division. For every w∈ℂ with |w|<1, HasDerivAt φ (2i/(1−w)²) w. For every z∈ℂ with Im z>0, HasDerivAt ψ (2i/(z+i)²) z, and [2i/(1−ψ(z))²]·[2i/(z+i)²]=1.
subproblem.lean_statement: (∀ w : ℂ, ‖w‖ < 1 → HasDerivAt (fun u : ℂ => Complex.I * (1 + u) / (1 - u)) (2 * Complex.I / (1 - w) ^ 2) w) ∧ (∀ z : ℂ, 0 < z.im → HasDerivAt (fun u : ℂ => (u - Complex.I) / (u + Complex.I)) (2 * Complex.I / (z + Complex.I) ^ 2) z) ∧ (∀ z : ℂ, 0 < z.im → (2 * Complex.I / (1 - (z - Complex.I) / (z + Complex.I)) ^ 2) * (2 * Complex.I / (z + Complex.I) ^ 2) = 1)
subproblem.natural_proof:
1. Define φ(u)=i(1+u)/(1−u) and ψ(u)=(u−i)/(u+i). If |w|<1, then 1−w≠0, since equality would force w=1 of norm 1.
2. The functions u↦i(1+u) and u↦1−u have ordinary complex derivatives i and −1. The complex quotient rule at w gives HasDerivAt φ [(i(1−w)−i(1+w)(−1))/(1−w)²] w. The numerator equals i[(1−w)+(1+w)]=2i, yielding the first asserted derivative.
3. If Im z>0, then z+i≠0 since its imaginary part is Im z+1>0. Both affine functions u↦u−i and u↦u+i have ordinary complex derivative 1. Their quotient therefore has derivative [(z+i)−(z−i)]/(z+i)²=2i/(z+i)² at z, yielding the second asserted derivative.
4. For this z, let s=z+i and t=1−ψ(z). Calculation over s≠0 gives t=[(z+i)−(z−i)]/s=2i/s. Thus t≠0 and ts=2i. Consequently t²s²=(2i)²≠0, and [2i/t²]·[2i/s²]=(2i)²/(t²s²)=(2i)²/(2i)²=1. This is exactly the asserted derivative-factor identity and completes all three conclusions.
proof_key_steps: Establish the nonzero denominator on the disk and apply the quotient rule to φ.
Simplify the forward derivative numerator to 2i.
Establish z+i≠0 on the upper half-plane and apply the quotient rule to ψ.
Use 1−ψ(z)=2i/(z+i) to prove the derivative-factor product equals one.

subproblem.title: The Cayley maps identify the unit disk and upper half-plane
subproblem.statement: Define φ(w)=i(1+w)/(1−w) and ψ(z)=(z−i)/(z+i) for all complex arguments using total complex division. Let D={w∈ℂ : |w|<1} and H={z∈ℂ : Im z>0}. Then φ maps D into H, ψ maps H into D, φ(ψ(z))=z for every z∈H, and ψ(φ(w))=w for every w∈D.
subproblem.lean_statement: (∀ w : ℂ, ‖w‖ < 1 → 0 < (Complex.I * (1 + w) / (1 - w)).im) ∧ (∀ z : ℂ, 0 < z.im → ‖(z - Complex.I) / (z + Complex.I)‖ < 1) ∧ (∀ z : ℂ, 0 < z.im → Complex.I * (1 + (z - Complex.I) / (z + Complex.I)) / (1 - (z - Complex.I) / (z + Complex.I)) = z) ∧ (∀ w : ℂ, ‖w‖ < 1 → (Complex.I * (1 + w) / (1 - w) - Complex.I) / (Complex.I * (1 + w) / (1 - w) + Complex.I) = w)
subproblem.natural_proof:
1. Define φ(w)=i(1+w)/(1−w) and ψ(z)=(z−i)/(z+i) on all of ℂ using total complex division. Fix w with |w|<1. Then 1−w≠0, since otherwise w=1, contradicting |w|<1.
2. Write w=x+iy, and put q=(1−x)²+y²=|1−w|²>0. Multiplying numerator and denominator of φ(w) by (1−x)+iy gives φ(w)=[−2y+i(1−x²−y²)]/q. Since x²+y²=|w|²<1, its imaginary part (1−x²−y²)/q is positive. This proves φ(D)⊆H.
3. Fix z=x+iy with y>0. Its denominator s=z+i is nonzero because Im s=y+1>0. Put p=x²+(y+1)²>0 and r=x²+(y−1)². Then p−r=4y>0. Multiplicativity of the complex norm gives |ψ(z)|²=r/p<1. Since |ψ(z)|≥0, this implies |ψ(z)|<1, proving ψ(H)⊆D.
4. For this z, computation over the nonzero denominator s gives 1+ψ(z)=2z/s and 1−ψ(z)=2i/s. The latter is nonzero because 2i and s are nonzero. Consequently φ(ψ(z))=i(2z/s)/(2i/s)=z by field cancellation.
5. For w with |w|<1, put t=1−w≠0. Subtraction and addition over this denominator give φ(w)−i=2iw/t and φ(w)+i=2i/t≠0. Hence ψ(φ(w))=(2iw/t)/(2i/t)=w. Together, these prove all four conclusions.
proof_key_steps: Show 1−w is nonzero on the unit disk.
Expand the imaginary part of φ(w) and prove it positive.
Compare squared norms of z−i and z+i to show ψ(z) lies in the disk.
Compute 1±ψ(z) and cancel nonzero factors to obtain φ(ψ(z))=z.
Compute φ(w)±i and cancel nonzero factors to obtain ψ(φ(w))=w.
